title: Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017
short_title: Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017

divisions.question: The majority voted against a [motion](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Hansard/Hansard_Display?bid=chamber/hansardr/a923c04b-f8ae-47fa-a4b3-94f3cba5886d/&sid=0000) to reject the main idea of the bills. In parliamentary jargon, they voted against refusing to read the bills for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that the House can continue to consider the bills. ### What is the bills' main idea? The bills were introduced to establish the First Home Super Saver Scheme. Together they will: * *enable first home savers to make voluntary contributions into the superannuation system and to withdraw those contributions and associated earnings for the purposes of purchasing their first home;* * *allow an individual aged 65 years or over to use the proceeds of one sale of their main residence to make contributions (downsizer contributions) of up to $300 000 to their superannuation; and* * *impose a first home super saver tax on individuals who have not entered into a contract to purchase or construct their first home or recontributed the required amount into superannuation.* Read more about the bills and their purpose in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd043). ### Motion text > *That all words after 'That' be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *'The House declines to give the bill and related bill a second reading as:* > *(1) the First Home Super Saver Scheme will do nothing to address housing affordability but will instead work to undermine Australia’s world class superannuation system; and* > *(2) any housing affordability package that does not include reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax is a sham.'*

The majority agreed with the bills' main idea, which means they can now discuss them in more detail. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bills for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What is the bills' main idea? The bills were introduced to establish the First Home Super Saver Scheme. Together they will: * *enable first home savers to make voluntary contributions into the superannuation system and to withdraw those contributions and associated earnings for the purposes of purchasing their first home;* * *allow an individual aged 65 years or over to use the proceeds of one sale of their main residence to make contributions (downsizer contributions) of up to $300 000 to their superannuation; and* * *impose a first home super saver tax on individuals who have not entered into a contract to purchase or construct their first home or recontributed the required amount into superannuation.* Read more about the bills and their purpose in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd043).

The majority voted in favour of [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-12-05.8.2) to the [Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5960), which were moved by NSW Senator [David Leyonhjelm](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/nsw/david_leyonhjelm). ### What do these amendments do? Senator Leyonhjelm [explained that](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-12-05.8.2): > *The government's First Home Super Saver Scheme allows taxpayers to make one withdrawal in their lifetime from their voluntary superannuation contributions to purchase their first and only home. Item 2 of my amendments provides an exemption to the requirement it be a first home. The exemption will apply if the tax commissioner determines that the taxpayer has suffered financial hardship, the circumstances of which can be determined by regulation. I envisage that regulations would refer to circumstances where a taxpayer has limited savings, is currently renting and had an interest in a home many years ago in a cheaper real estate market or when a taxpayer was in a relationship that has since broken down. Taxpayers will still be limited to one withdrawal of their voluntary superannuation in their lifetime and it must be for their only home. This amendment will help people who are struggling to leave the rental market and buy their own home in the face of high property prices. The fact that they once owned their own home, possibly some decades ago, does not make their struggle any less stressful.* ### Amendment text > *(1) Page 2 (after line 11) , after clause 3 , insert:* >> *4 Review of operation of amendments* >> *(1) The Minister must cause an independent review of the operation of the amendments made by this Act.* >> *(2) The review must:* >>> *(a) start as soon as practicable after 18 months after Royal Assent; and

speeches.speaker: Michael Sukkar
speeches.brief: The bill introduces the First Home Super Saver Scheme tax under schedule 1 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No.1) Bill 2017, aimed at removing the incentive to withdraw funds without purchasing a first home or recontributing to superannuation.

speeches.speaker: Chris Bowen
speeches.brief: The Labor Party opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, arguing it would worsen housing affordability and undermine retirement incomes, and criticised the government for failing to reform negative gearing, noting that 50% of negative gearing and 70% of capital gains tax concessions go to the top 10% of income earners.

speeches.speaker: Chris Bowen
speeches.brief: The Labor Party will strongly oppose the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, arguing it undermines Australia's superannuation system and will worsen housing affordability by pushing up demand. Labor moved a second reading amendment stating the First Home Super Saver Scheme will not address housing affordability and that any package without reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax is a sham.

speeches.speaker: Luke Howarth
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017 and the First Home Super Saver Tax Bill 2017, promoting the First Home Super Saver Scheme and downsizing barriers as measures to help first home buyers. They criticised the shadow Treasurer, the member for McMahon, for opposing the bill and accused him of lying about it undermining Australian superannuation.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wallace
speeches.brief: The speech supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, which includes the First Home Super Saver Scheme (allowing up to $30,000 in voluntary super contributions for a deposit), a downsizing incentive for over-65s (up to $300,000 per person into super), a vacancy tax on foreign owners of residential property not occupied or rented for at least six months, and the removal of travel expense deductions and limits on plant and equipment depreciation to new assets.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment bills, arguing that the super saver scheme for first home buyers is a dangerous tinker that fails to address the core drivers of unaffordability—negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions, which respectively benefit the top 10% of earners by 50% and 70%. They supported the downsizing measure (allowing over-65s to contribute up to $300,000 from home sale proceeds) but rejected the combined bill, citing local price surges (Malabar homes rose 46% to a $2 million average; Coogee to $2.4 million).

speeches.speaker: Andrew Broad
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017 would help young Australians save for a home deposit by allowing voluntary superannuation contributions of up to $15,000 per year (capped at $30,000) and incentivise seniors to downsize by permitting a non-concessional contribution of up to $300,000 from the sale of their home into super. The speaker also proposed capping negative gearing deductions at $30,000 per year and urged banks to consider three years of rental history as proof of loan eligibility.

speeches.speaker: Susan Templeman
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, arguing it fails to address negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions—which benefit the top 10% of income earners by 50% and 70% respectively—and noted that rental stress in the Blue Mountains is three times higher than in Woollahra. The speaker called for increased social housing, inclusionary zoning, and other measures, citing criticism from the Grattan Institute and UNSW Professor Richard Holden.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Support was expressed for the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, which would allow up to $15,000 per year and $30,000 total in voluntary superannuation contributions for first home deposits, and a downsizing cap of $300,000 (or $600,000 per couple) for those aged 65 and over selling a primary residence held for 10 years. The opposition, including the member for Macquarie, was accused of opposing the bill due to union ties rather than supporting young Australians.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the housing affordability bills, which allow first home buyers to use superannuation contributions for a deposit (capped at $15,000 per year and $30,000 total), reduce revenue by $250 million, and permit older Australians to downsize with super contributions up to $300,000 or $600,000 for couples, while also introducing a foreign-resident vacancy tax, a 50% cap on foreign ownership in new developments, and $117.2 million for homelessness services.

speeches.speaker: Emma McBride
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017 and the First Home Super Saver Tax Bill 2017, arguing they fail to address negative gearing and capital gains tax reform and would undermine superannuation. They supported Labor's alternative plan, including building 55,000 new homes over three years, creating 25,000 jobs annually, a bond aggregator for affordable rental housing, a vacant property tax, and $88 million for a safe housing fund.

speeches.speaker: Ross Hart
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, arguing its First Home Super Saver Scheme would increase demand and housing prices rather than improve affordability, and called instead for reform of negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts. The speaker noted support for the downsizing measure if separated from the bill, and cited that nearly 70% of Australians are concerned they will never own a home, with 875,000 households in housing stress.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the First Home Super Saver Scheme, arguing superannuation was designed for retirement, not home buying, and criticised the government for failing to reform negative gearing and capital gains tax, which largely benefit high-income earners. They highlighted record median house prices in the ACT ($723,980) and Sydney ($1 million), cited data showing close to 70% of Australians are concerned about home ownership, and called for appointing a Minister for Housing and Homelessness and exploring innovative housing models like the Nightingale project and YWCA’s Lady Heydon House to address a looming homelessness crisis, particularly among older women.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment bill is a sham that will not improve housing affordability, and criticised the government for inaction while noting that 13,000 workers in the Lalor electorate have been affected by penalty rate cuts. They proposed Labor’s policies to limit negative gearing to new homes and reform capital gains tax, claiming these would provide $32 billion over 10 years and reduce housing price pressure.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government’s housing bills were ineffective bandaids that would not fix the housing affordability crisis, instead repeating Labor’s policy to limit negative gearing to new housing and reduce the capital gains tax discount. They cited statistics such as Melbourne’s median house price at $880,902, only 40% of 25–34-year-olds owning a home, and negative gearing costing $10 billion annually, while praising Victorian Labor’s rental reforms.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government's bill fails to address Australia's housing affordability crisis, citing that house prices have risen 60 times in Sydney since 1970 while wages only increased 15 times, and criticised the First Home Super Saver Scheme for forcing a choice between home ownership and retirement savings, while supporting the downsizing measure for over-65s. The speaker also noted that 217,000 families are on social housing waiting lists and that tax concessions for property investors total $43 billion annually compared to $5 billion for social housing, calling for reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts.

speeches.speaker: Julie Owens
speeches.brief: The speaker criticised the government for a belated and inadequate response to the housing affordability crisis, noting that homeownership among 25–34 year olds fell from 60% to under 40% over 30 years and that tax concessions have driven price acceleration. The government's bill includes the First Home Super Saver Scheme, which lets first home buyers withdraw voluntary super contributions for a deposit.

speeches.speaker: Peter Khalil
speeches.brief: Labor opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No 1) Bill 2017, arguing it was ineffective and only paid lip service to the housing crisis, noting home ownership rates for 25–34 year olds fell from 60% to 48%.

speeches.speaker: Julian Hill
speeches.brief: The government's housing affordability package was criticised as a sham with no meaningful measures, particularly the first home buyer super saver scheme described as regressive and damaging. The speaker argued that the government refuses to address tax concessions for negative gearing and capital gains tax, which inflate investor demand and lock out first home buyers, while Labor proposes to reform those concessions.

acts.title: Treasury Laws Amendment (Reducing Pressure on Housing Affordability Measures No. 1) Act 2017
